common_name: Hoshi-zora Cast Iron Plant (Starry Sky Speckled Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; this old Japanese heirloom is grown for its foliage pattern rather than its hidden purple-and-cream spring flowers.

directions: Set divisions into rich, well-drained soil in bright to deep shade, sheltered from direct sun that will bleach or scorch the leaves. Hoshi-zora, whose name means starry sky, produces long dark green blades lightly dusted with small cream-to-yellow flecks across the whole leaf rather than in bold stripes, giving established clumps a soft, glimmering texture at eye level. Growth is slow and clumping, so plants rarely need dividing except to propagate; remove any leaf that reverts to solid green to keep the speckling consistent. Once rooted in, it tolerates the same deep dry shade and root competition that fells most other shade perennials, needing only occasional grooming of aged foliage each year.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Gold Lancer Cast Iron Plant (Yellow-Banded Narrow-Leaf Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to deep shade; the narrow, pendent leaf tips give this Sichuan selection a finer, more graceful profile than broad-leaved cast iron plants.

directions: Grow in consistently shaded, humus-rich soil, since exposure to direct sun will scorch the narrow, lance-shaped leaves. Gold Lancer, a Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction, carries a broad yellow central band down each dark green, downward-arching leaf, creating strong color contrast without the bulk of wider-leaved aspidistra cultivars. It is slow to spread, so plant it where its narrow vertical habit can be appreciated up close, such as along a shaded path edge or in a container. Established clumps are drought-tolerant and essentially pest-free, needing only an annual clearing of aged leaves to stay tidy.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Spek-tacular Cast Iron Plant (Stably Speckled Sichuan Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this Sichuan market find was selected because its yellow speckling holds steady rather than fading with age.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in part shade to deep shade, where its tall, upright leaves can arch freely without crowding. Spek-tacular was singled out among speckled Aspidistra sichuanensis seedlings for spotting that stays crisp and stable year after year instead of washing out, giving clumps a consistently dramatic, dotted appearance. It is among the taller cast iron plant selections, so give it extra room at the back of a shaded border or beneath high-canopy trees. Like other aspidistra, it is deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and needs little beyond occasional removal of tattered old leaves.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Rawhide Cast Iron Plant (Thick-Textured Yellow-Spotted Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep shade; this collector's selection was traced to a Japanese variegated-plant collection before entering the American nursery trade.

directions: Site in deep shade in humus-rich soil, as with all cast iron plants direct sun will quickly scorch the foliage. Rawhide is named for its unusually thick, stiff leaf texture, almost like hard plastic, likely the result of a natural ploidy change, and its blades are heavily dusted with yellow spotting. The clump stays comparatively compact and slow-spreading, making it a good choice for a shaded container or a tight woodland planting pocket. It shares the extreme drought tolerance and low maintenance of other aspidistra, needing only occasional removal of leaves once they age past two or three years.

common_name: Spotty Cast Iron Plant (Irregularly Yellow-Spotted Sichuan Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; this Cistus Nursery seedling selection was chosen for its bold, irregular yellow spotting.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright to deep shade, avoiding any direct sun that would scorch the leaves. Spotty bears large, irregularly shaped, muted yellow spots scattered unevenly across each dark green blade, giving every leaf a slightly different pattern rather than a uniform speckle. Clumps build slowly into a dense architectural mass useful for year-round texture beneath trees or along a shaded foundation. As with other cast iron plants, established clumps tolerate heavy root competition and drought and require only occasional cleanup of old foliage.

common_name: Gilt Edge Toad Lily (Creamy Yellow-Margined Formosa Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the creamy leaf margins are showy well before the pink freckled flowers open in late summer.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, where the compact foliage clump can widen gradually by rhizome. Gilt Edge is grown as much for its glossy, dark green leaves rimmed in creamy yellow as for its late-season bloom, since the variegation stays attractive from spring through frost. In late summer to early fall, arching stems carry pale pink, purple-freckled, orchid-like flowers in the upper leaf axils, extending shade-garden color into autumn. Keep soil evenly moist through summer and mulch with leaf litter over winter; clumps are slow to spread and rarely need division except to propagate.

common_name: Golden Gleam Toad Lily (Chartreuse Grey-Spotted Hairy Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; foliage color is brightest in cooler climates and tends to green up in hot summers.

directions: Site in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright to partial shade, since strong afternoon sun will fade the distinctive foliage color. Golden Gleam, a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction, emerges with chartreuse leaves heavily dotted in grey, a striking combination before the plant even flowers. Compact and low-growing compared to most toad lilies, it fits well toward the front of a shaded bed or in a container, where its bicolor foliage carries the display for months ahead of the dark purple, white-speckled flowers that crowd the upper leaf axils in fall. Keep soil consistently moist through summer and top-dress with compost each spring; clumps expand slowly and divide easily if a larger patch is wanted.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox

common_name: Autumn Glow Toad Lily (Wide Gold-Margined Formosa Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Japanese selection was bred for the cut-flower trade and forms a substantial patch within a few seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, allowing room for the vigorous clump to widen by rhizome over several years. Autumn Glow carries an unusually wide, bright yellow border around each dark green leaf, among the most dramatic variegation of any formosana selection, so the foliage alone earns it a place in the shade border. Starting in midsummer and continuing into fall, upright stems bear clusters of amethyst-purple, dark-spotted, orchid-like flowers above the variegated foliage. Water regularly through dry spells and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom and crisp leaf color.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, partly shaded to shaded site; protect from harsh sun and drying wind while the thick rootstock establishes.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with partial to full shade, out of drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Marginata carries sturdy, upright, leathery leaves each traced with a narrow, clean creamy-white margin, giving the classic Rohdea rosette a refined, hand-edged look distinct from the plain green species. Growth is very slow, so choose a permanent position; inconspicuous flowers hidden near the base in fall are followed by long-lasting red berries on mature plants. Watch for slugs and snails, which favor the thick fleshy foliage, and otherwise expect an almost maintenance-free evergreen accent for the deepest shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox

common_name: Shiro Botan Sacred Lily (White-Variegated Collector's Omoto)

planting.note: Plant small divisions in rich, well-drained soil in part sun to full shade; variegation intensifies with the new leaf flush in late spring and early summer.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to full shade, siting it where its slow-forming rosette can be appreciated up close as a collector's specimen. Shiro Botan, prized among Japanese omoto cultivars, produces strong white variegation across nearly every leaf, with the pattern becoming most vivid as each new flush of foliage matures through early summer. Like other Rohdea, it is extremely slow-growing and long-lived, tolerating deep, dry shade once established but rewarding steady moisture and light feeding with fuller variegated growth. Divide only when necessary to propagate, since disturbing the thick rootstock sets growth back for a season or more.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox

common_name: Mure Suzume Sacred Lily (Flock-of-Sparrows Variegated Omoto)

planting.note: Plant small divisions in rich, well-drained soil in part sun to full shade; the fine white striping is most visible on spring and summer growth and fades somewhat in winter.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to full shade, giving this collector's cultivar a protected spot away from harsh sun or drying wind. Mure Suzume, its name translating loosely as flock of sparrows, bears thin white variegation lines running through each leaf and thickening toward the margins, creating a delicate, hand-painted texture on the glossy evergreen rosette. The variegation shows most strongly on spring and summer flushes and becomes subtler through winter dormancy, though the plant remains evergreen year-round. As with other Rohdea, expect very slow growth and long lifespan, with best results from consistent light moisture and minimal disturbance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox
